analysis.one_liner: Sets federal health and safety standards, inspections, and penalties for private teen boot camps and therapeutic boarding schools.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 322-47 on June 25, 2008, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Private residential programs for troubled teens — wilderness camps, boot camps, and therapeutic boarding schools — were largely unregulated in many states, and children had died or been abused in them. This bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to set minimum health and safety standards covering abuse bans, restraints, phone access, staff background checks, and disclosure to parents; to run unannounced inspections at least every two years; to publish each program's violations and child deaths on a public website; to run a national abuse complaint hotline; and to fine operators up to $50,000 per violation. It would also let families sue over violations and tie federal child-abuse-prevention grants to states putting equivalent licensing in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Teens placed in private residential programs for emotional, behavioral, or substance-abuse problems, and their parents, who currently send children into facilities with little independent oversight and often cannot see a program's history of violations or deaths.

how_it_helps.text: Bans child abuse and neglect, withholding of essential food, water, shelter, or medical care, and humiliating or degrading treatment in covered programs [S4].
Limits physical restraints and seclusion and requires reasonable phone access, so children can reach home and reporting hotlines [S4].
Requires criminal history checks and sex-offender registry searches for every staff member and volunteer, disqualifying people with violent or child-abuse felony convictions [S4].

Requires unannounced site inspections of each program location at least every two years, civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, referral of violations to the Attorney General, and a private right of action allowing families to sue for damages [S4].

Requires a public federal website listing each program's violations, penalties, court judgments, and any deaths of children in its care, plus a national toll-free hotline for abuse complaints that triggers an investigation within 30 days [S4].

Conditions federal child-abuse-prevention grants on states adopting health and safety licensing for covered programs, with their own inspections, databases, and graduated sanctions like fines and license revocation [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of private wilderness camps, boot camps, and therapeutic boarding schools, who would face federal standards, unannounced inspections, fines, public disclosure of violations and deaths, and lawsuits; plus taxpayers for the authorized funding ($50 million a year for the HHS side and $200 million a year added to state grant funding through 2013) [S4].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs — background checks, trained staff, inspections readiness — would fall hardest on small programs, and some could close, reducing placement options for parents of severely troubled children [S4].

The bill creates a new federal inspection and enforcement bureaucracy and authorizes substantial spending — $50 million a year for the Act plus $200 million a year added to state grants, totaling $1.25 billion over five years [S4].

The private right of action with punitive damages and attorneys' fees would expose operators to lawsuits, which supporters see as accountability and critics as a litigation burden; the bill also overrides the usual limits on such suits in institutional-rights cases [S4].

During floor debate, Rep. Michele Bachmann pushed to require that parents give consent before any prescription medication is administered to a child in a program, reflecting concern about how programs handle medication; the House instead considered the committee's version with its own parental-notification requirements for medication changes and missed doses [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a documented harm — abuse, neglect, and deaths of children in programs marketed to desperate parents with little oversight — with disclosure, inspections, and enforcement rather than banning the industry. Its costs are real but modest: compliance spending by operators, about $250 million a year in authorizations, and added litigation. The main design gap is that it leans on federal standards only until states build their own licensing, which is slower and weaker than permanent state-level oversight in some states.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill on June 25, 2008, but the Senate referred it to its Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee ordered the bill reported on a 27-16 vote on May 14, 2008, and it was reported May 22 with an amendment [S6].

The House debated the bill under a structured rule on June 24, 2008, adopted the committee's substitute, and took up a motion by Rep. Michele Bachmann to recommit with instructions requiring parental consent before prescription medication is administered [S6].
The House passed the bill 322-47 on June 25, 2008 [S1].
The Senate received the bill but its committee never reported it, and it received no vote before the Congress ended [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and operators of private teen residential programs, who avoided federal standards, unannounced inspections, public disclosure of violations and deaths, fines, and lawsuits for the rest of the 110th Congress and beyond; parents and teens remained without federal protections.

against.what_they_did: The industry pressed to keep the troubled-teen market free of federal oversight, as the bill would have imposed inspections, penalties, and public disclosure on it

sides.party_line_note: The bill was Democratic-sponsored with all-Democratic cosponsors, but it cleared committee 27-16 and passed the House 322-47 with votes from both parties.

industries.industry: Private residential youth treatment programs (wilderness camps, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools)
industries.note: The bill would put these operators under federal health and safety standards, unannounced inspections, up to $50,000 fines per violation, a public record of violations and child deaths, and civil suits by harmed families. Its interest in staying outside that regime runs against the safety of the children enrolled there.

States would have to build licensing, inspection, database, and enforcement systems for covered programs to keep receiving federal child-abuse-prevention grants, an added administrative burden tied to additional federal funding ($200 million a year).
